cim_eredeti: Golis: Dear Mr. President: Money isn’t everything
szoveg_eredeti:
“The future of AI will be decided by a few dozen people.”

— Cover of last week’s New York magazine

In a TV interview last week, President Donald Trump dismissed warnings that artificial intelligence may bring unintended consequences. He said artificial intelligence development must continue so American companies can keep pace with Chinese companies.

Following the meeting with Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese leader Xi Jinping on Thursday, we wait to find out whether efforts to regulate AI are merely window dressing or something more substantial. I know. People appreciate the conveniences associated with AI. Whether it will leave millions of people jobless or run off and do God-knows-what will be determined at a later date.

With his usual modesty, Trump wrote on Truth Social: “The only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, TV and the USA has that, in spades!”

Meanwhile, one of Trump’s key advisors on AI matters — Nvidia Chief Executive Officer Jensen Huang — resigned after it was disclosed he had extra-marital affairs with a company employee and a second woman alleged to be a Chinese spy. It’s not a good look for Huang, stock prices, Trump or for AI.

Huang was, The New York Times said, “the face of the AI boom powering the US economy.”

And so here we are, talking to bots and otherwise appreciating help from AI, but wondering, too, if it will run amok.

It’s worth noting that the original warnings Trump dismissed didn’t come from some fuzzy-headed liberals. The warnings came from the CEOs of the two companies leading the way on artificial intelligence — Anthropic (aka Claude) and Open AI (aka ChatGPT).

“We welcome a federal framework that sets consistent safety requirements for frontier AI,” Open AI CEO Sam Altman said on X. “No amount of American competitive pressure should justify recklessness.”

His supporters and detractors don’t agree on much, but there is this: President Donald Trump likes making money, and he likes the people who share his passion for making money.

If AI can be profitable, after all, what’s the problem?

Space doesn’t allow a listing of all the policy changes designed to reward the people the president likes.

The Trump administration has spent billions of your dollars to re-animate the coal industry, otherwise promote fossil fuels and discourage alternative sources of energy. The administration recently gave $120 million to a company in turn for the company’s promise not to install a wind farm on the Central California coast.

This is the administration that made plans to trade land in Yosemite National Park to a private developer. It shrank a national monument in Utah so that the land could be made available to mining companies and other businesses. It made plans to eviscerate the authority of the California Coastal Commission — the better to promote seaside subdivisions, nuclear plants, on-and offshore oil developments and Elon Musk’s rocket launches.

What’s made plain by all this is that Trump and his acolytes don’t like rules and customs designed to protect consumers, workers or the environment.

Do some of these rules offend common sense? Sure they do.

Does it make sense to sack them all? It seems common sense that a society would dump the rules that are not working and keep the rest. In the push and shove of politics, however, common sense sometimes gets lost.

While we wait to find out if artificial intelligence could set in motion a doomsday scenario, Trump has already told us what he thinks. Has he been known to change his mind? Well, yes.

Business and the jobs it creates are essential to a successful society, but they shouldn’t become a pretext for environmental destruction or favoring campaign donors over the public welfare.

In a recent column, I noted that America ranks 23rd in the world for happiness, even though it’s the most affluent country in the world if measured by the number of millionaires and billionaires.

In other countries, people with a lot less of everything — save what matters most — report being happier.

After a rash of network outages, some are wondering if societies have become too reliant on new technology.

One would think that governments would be in pursuit of a coherent and credible process for deciding if artificial intelligence poses risks. But at a time in which every conversation becomes politicized, we remain stuck in neutral.

Pete Golis is a columnist for The Press Democrat. Email him at golispd@gmail.com.
